subtype: Approach: hiding at home and skipping school [Pitfall]
passage: Come, sit, Meera. Let me tell you about my own stomach aches. I am Hemant, and when I was a boy of ten, another boy named Dinesh waited by the school gate every morning to snatch my cap. So I began groaning at breakfast. "My head, Aai, my stomach." Three days at home, warm blanket, no Dinesh. Lovely! By the fourth day the relief was gone and a heavy feeling had taken its place, because Monday was still coming. That evening my mother sat on my bed and said, "You are not really ill, are you? What is wrong?" Out it all came. She did not scold. She held my hand and said we would tell the teacher together.

qa.q: What did Dinesh do to Hemant every morning at the school gate?
qa.a: Dinesh waited at the school gate to snatch Hemant's cap.

qa.q: What was Hemant feeling on the fourth day at home?
qa.a: A heavy worry, because the relief had gone and Monday, and Dinesh, was still coming.

qa.q: What could Hemant have done instead of pretending to be ill, and why?
qa.a: He could have told his mother or a teacher on the first day, because adults could then deal with Dinesh and Hemant would not lose days of school.

qa.q: How might Hemant's mother have felt when he finally told her?
qa.a: Probably concerned, and glad that he trusted her, since she asked gently, did not scold and held his hand.

grounding: A boy fakes illness to avoid the bully, which gives short relief until his mother notices and asks what is wrong.
